title: Coverage and consensus
text:
Goal: Measure genome coverage, identify low-depth regions, build a consensus genome, and identify candidate variants.
We will analyze the SARS-CoV-2 sequencing run SRR26396743 from NCBI, using the trimmed reads and BAM file generated in the previous sessions.
Input files
If a previous step failed, use the corresponding precomputed files provided with the course, if available.

title: Coverage and consensus
section: Step 1 — Calculate mean depth and genome breadth at ≥10×

title: Coverage and consensus
section: Step 2 — Build the consensus genome with iVar
text:
Step 2 — Build the consensus genome with iVar
A consensus genome represents the most strongly supported nucleotide at each reference position, subject to the calling thresholds.
Here, we will use:

Minimum base quality: Q20
Minimum depth: 10 reads
Minimum proportion of reads supporting a base: 50%
Missing or insufficiently supported positions: N

Create the output directories:
mkdir -p results/coverage results/consensus results/variants
Run samtools mpileup and pass its output to ivar consensus:
samtools mpileup \
  -aa -A -d 0 -Q 0 \
  -f data/NC_045512.2.fasta \
  results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam \
  | ivar consensus \
      -p results/consensus/SRR26396743 \
      -q 20 \
      -t 0.5 \
      -m 10 \
      -n N






TipOptions












Command / Option
Explanation




samtools mpileup
Generates per-position alignment information from the BAM file.


-aa
Includes all reference positions, including positions with zero coverage.


-A
Includes anomalous read pairs/orphan reads that would otherwise be skipped.


-d 0
Removes the maximum depth limit.


-Q 0
Sets the minimum base quality threshold in mpileup to Q0.


-f data/NC_045512.2.fasta
Specifies the reference genome in FASTA format.


results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam
Input BAM file containing coordinate-sorted alignments.


ivar consensus
Generates a consensus sequence from the pileup data.


-p results/consensus/SRR26396743
Sets the output file prefix.


-q 20
Uses a minimum base quality of Q20 for consensus calling.


-t 0.5
Requires a minimum base frequency of 50% to call a consensus base.


-m 10
Requires at least 10 reads covering a position.


-n N
Uses N for positions where a consensus base cannot be called.






This produces a consensus FASTA file, normally named:
results/consensus/SRR26396743.fa
Inspect its header and sequence:
head -c 300 results/consensus/SRR26396743.fa

section: Step 3 — Measure the number of ambiguous bases

title: Coverage and consensus
section: Step 4 — Identify candidate variants with bcftools
text:
Step 4 — Identify candidate variants with bcftools
We will compare the aligned reads with the reference to identify candidate single-nucleotide variants and short insertions or deletions.
Generate a VCF file:
bcftools mpileup \
  -f data/NC_045512.2.fasta \
  -Q 20 \
  -d 1000000 \
  -a AD \
  results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam \
  | bcftools call \
      -mv \
      --ploidy 1 \
      -Oz \
      -o results/variants/SRR26396743.vcf.gz






TipOptions












Command / Option
Explanation




bcftools mpileup
Generates per-position read data for variant detection.


-f data/NC_045512.2.fasta
Specifies the reference genome in FASTA format.


-Q 20
Excludes bases with a base quality below Q20.


-d 1000000
Sets the maximum read depth per position to 1,000,000.


-a AD
Adds allele-depth (AD) information.


results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam
Input BAM file containing aligned reads.


bcftools call
Identifies candidate variants from the read data.


-m
Uses the multiallelic variant-calling model.


-v
Outputs variant sites only.


--ploidy 1
Assumes a haploid genome.


-Oz
Writes the VCF output in compressed BGZF format.


-o results/variants/SRR26396743.vcf.gz
Specifies the output VCF file.



Output: A compressed VCF file containing candidate variants identified by comparing the sequencing reads with the SARS-CoV-2 reference genome.



Index the VCF:
bcftools index results/variants/SRR26396743.vcf.gz
Display the variant records:
bcftools view -H results/variants/SRR26396743.vcf.gz \
  | cut -f1,2,4,5,6






Tip



The columns displayed are:

Reference sequence
Position
Reference allele
Alternative allele
Variant quality (QUAL)



Count the reported variant records:
bcftools view -H results/variants/SRR26396743.vcf.gz \
  | wc -l

title: Coverage and consensus
section: Step 5 — Change the consensus depth threshold
text:
Step 5 — Change the consensus depth threshold
A higher minimum depth can make the consensus more conservative, but it can also increase the number of ambiguous bases.
Build a second consensus requiring at least 30 reads per position:
samtools mpileup \
  -aa -A -d 0 -Q 0 \
  -f data/NC_045512.2.fasta \
  results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam \
  | ivar consensus \
      -p results/consensus/SRR26396743.m30 \
      -q 20 \
      -t 0.5 \
      -m 30 \
      -n N
Count the ambiguous bases in the second consensus:
grep -v '^>' results/consensus/SRR26396743.m30.fa \
  | tr -cd 'N' \
  | wc -c
Compare the results with the consensus generated at 10×.

title: Coverage and consensus
section: Step 6 — Is this genome good enough?
text:
Step 6 — Is this genome good enough?
A genome is not simply “good” or “bad”: it is good enough for a specific purpose, based on several quality metrics.

title: Coverage and consensus
text:
The numbers that matter







Metric
Why it matters




Total reads / % mapped
Indicates the amount of sequencing data and the proportion mapping to the virus. A low mapping rate may indicate contamination or poor enrichment.


Mean depth
Indicates the average sequencing coverage at each reference position.


% of genome at ≥ 10× depth
Measures how much of the genome has sufficient coverage for reliable consensus calling.


% N / longest run of Ns
Indicates missing sequence information. Long runs of Ns may correspond to missing genomic regions.


Negative control (NTC)
Checks whether viral reads are detected in a sample that should contain no viral material.

title: From FASTQ to assembly: QC, trimming, assembly and identification
text:
Step 1 — Look at a read
A FASTQ file stores four lines per read: the read identifier, nucleotide sequence, a + separator, and a quality string. The files are compressed (.gz), so we use zcat.
zcat data/SRR26396743_1.fastq.gz | head -4
Questions

Which line contains the nucleotide sequence? Which contains the quality scores?
What does each character in the quality string represent?







TipAnswers






Line 1 is the read identifier, line 2 is the nucleotide sequence, line 3 is +, and line 4 contains the quality string.
Each quality character encodes the estimated confidence in the corresponding base.
crumbs: From FASTQ to assembly: QC, trimming, assembly and identification

title: From FASTQ to assembly: QC, trimming, assembly and identification
section: Step 2 — Quality control of the raw reads (FastQC + MultiQC)
text:
Step 2 — Quality control of the raw reads (FastQC + MultiQC)
FastQC analyzes individual FASTQ files and produces HTML reports. MultiQC combines the results into a single report.
Create an output directory:
mkdir -p results/qc_raw
Run FastQC:
fastqc -t 2 -o results/qc_raw data/SRR26396743_*.fastq.gz
Combine the reports:
multiqc results/qc_raw -o results/qc_raw
Open the report in your browser:
open results/qc_raw/multiqc_report.html
On Linux, you can use:
xdg-open results/qc_raw/multiqc_report.html
Examine three sections:

General Statistics: number of reads, sequence length, and overall quality indicators.
Per base sequence quality: quality distribution along the reads.
Adapter Content: evidence of adapter sequences remaining in the reads.
crumbs: From FASTQ to assembly: QC, trimming, assembly and identification

title: From FASTQ to assembly: QC, trimming, assembly and identification
text:
Step 3 — Trim reads with trimmomatic
trimmomatic can detect adapters in paired-end data, trim low-quality tails, filter short reads.
Create the output directories:
mkdir -p results/trimmed results/trimmomatic
Run trimmomatic:
trimmomatic PE \
  -threads 2 \
  -phred33 \
  data/SRR26396743_1.fastq.gz \
  data/SRR26396743_2.fastq.gz \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_1_paired.fastq.gz \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_1_unpaired.fastq.gz \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_2_paired.fastq.gz \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_2_unpaired.fastq.gz \
  TRAILING:20 \
  SLIDINGWINDOW:4:20 \
  MINLEN:50
What do the options mean?

PE: Processes paired-end reads.
-threads 2: Uses two CPU threads.
-phred33: Specifies the Phred+33 quality score encoding.
TRAILING:20: Removes low-quality bases from the ends of reads when their quality score is below 20.
SLIDINGWINDOW:4:20: Trims a read when the average quality score in a four-base sliding window falls below 20.
MINLEN:50: Discards reads shorter than 50 bases after trimming.
paired: Output files containing reads whose mates both pass filtering.
unpaired: Output files containing reads whose mates do not both pass filtering.
crumbs: From FASTQ to assembly: QC, trimming, assembly and identification

title: From FASTQ to assembly: QC, trimming, assembly and identification
text:
Step 4 — Check the trimmed reads
Run FastQC on the cleaned files:
mkdir -p results/qc_trimmed
fastqc -t 2 -o results/qc_trimmed results/trimmed/*.fastq.gz
Combine the reports:
multiqc results/qc_trimmed -o results/qc_trimmed
Open the report:
open results/qc_trimmed/multiqc_report.html
Compare the raw and trimmed reports.

title: From FASTQ to assembly: QC, trimming, assembly and identification
section: Step 5 — Assemble the reads with SPAdes
text:
Step 5 — Assemble the reads with SPAdes
An assembler joins overlapping reads into longer sequences called contigs. When paired-end information links contigs together, they can be ordered into scaffolds. SPAdes builds a de Bruijn graph from the reads and uses the R1/R2 pairing to resolve ambiguities.
Run SPAdes on the trimmed reads:
spades.py \
  -1 results/trimmed/SRR26396743_1_paired.fastq.gz \
  -2 results/trimmed/SRR26396743_2_paired.fastq.gz \
  --meta \
  -t 2 \
  -o results/spades



Option
Purpose




-1, -2
Trimmed R1 and R2 files (paired reads)


--meta
metagenomic mode


-t 2
Use two threads


-o
Output directory



When SPAdes finishes, look at the output folder:
ls results/spades
The main files are:

contigs.fasta: assembled contigs
scaffolds.fasta: contigs linked into scaffolds using paired-end information
spades.log: log of the run

List the five longest contigs:
seqkit sort -l -r results/spades/contigs.fasta | seqkit fx2tab -n -l | head -5

title: From FASTQ to assembly: QC, trimming, assembly and identification
section: Step 6 — Which organisms are in the reads? (Kraken2 or BLAST)
text:
Step 6 — Which organisms are in the reads? (Kraken2 or BLAST)
Assembling is not enough: we must verify that the sequences really come from the expected organism, and detect possible contamination (human DNA, bacteria, other viruses). Two complementary approaches are available.

Option A — Kraken2 on the reads
Kraken2 assigns a taxonomic label to each read by comparing its k-mers to a reference database. It is fast and gives an overview of all the organisms in the sample.
Create the output directory:
mkdir -p results/kraken2
Run Kraken2 on the trimmed read pairs. Replace db/kraken2 with the path of the Kraken2 database provided for the course:
kraken2 \
  --db db/kraken2 \
  --paired \
  --gzip-compressed \
  --threads 2 \
  --report results/kraken2/SRR26396743.report \
  --output results/kraken2/SRR26396743.kraken \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_1.fastq.gz \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_2.fastq.gz
Look at the taxonomic summary:
head -20 results/kraken2/SRR26396743.report
The report has six columns: percentage of reads in the clade, number of reads in the clade, number of reads assigned directly to the taxon, rank code (U unclassified, D domain, G genus, S species, …), NCBI taxonomy ID, and scientific name.
Show only the species-level lines, sorted by percentage:
awk '$4=="S"' results/kraken2/SRR26396743.report | sort -k1,1nr | head -10
Note: a complete Kraken2 database (e.g. Standard) is very large. For this practical, a small database (such as a viral or MiniKraken index) is sufficient. Indexes are listed at https://benlangmead.github.io/aws-indexes/k2.


Option B — BLAST on the contigs
BLAST aligns a sequence against a reference database and reports the best matches. It is slower but more precise, and works well on a few long contigs.
Extract the longest contig:
seqkit sort -l -r results/spades/contigs.fasta | seqkit head -n 1 > results/spades/longest_contig.fasta
Run blastn against the NCBI nucleotide database (remote search, internet connection required):
blastn \
  -query results/spades/longest_contig.fasta \
  -db nt \
  -remote \
  -max_target_seqs 5 \
  -outfmt "6 qseqid sseqid stitle pident length evalue bitscore" \
  -out results/spades/longest_contig.blast.tsv
cat results/spades/longest_contig.blast.tsv
The columns are: query ID, subject ID, subject title, percent identity, alignment length, E-value, and bit score.
You can also paste the sequence into the web interface: https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi (choose Nucleotide BLAST).

title: From FASTQ to assembly: QC, trimming, assembly and identification
section: Step 7 — Evaluate the assembly with QUAST
text:
Step 7 — Evaluate the assembly with QUAST
QUAST computes statistics describing an assembly. When a reference genome is provided, it also measures how much of the reference is covered by the assembly.
Create the output directory and run QUAST. Replace the reference path with the SARS-CoV-2 reference genome (NC_045512.2) provided in the course folder:
mkdir -p results/quast
quast.py \
  results/spades/contigs.fasta \
  results/spades/scaffolds.fasta \
  -r data/NC_045512.2.fasta \
  --min-contig 200 \
  -t 2 \
  -o results/quast







Option
Purpose




-r
Reference genome (needed for genome fraction, misassemblies, NGA50)


--min-contig 200
Ignore contigs shorter than 200 bp


-t 2
Use two threads


-o
Output directory



Display the text report and open the HTML report:
cat results/quast/report.txt
open results/quast/report.html






TipInterpretation





Key Assembly Quality Metrics

1. Assembly statistics (reference-independent)
These metrics describe the assembled sequences without requiring a reference genome.







Metric
Meaning




# contigs
Number of assembled contigs meeting the specified minimum length. Fewer contigs can indicate a more continuous assembly.


Largest contig
Length of the longest assembled contig, in base pairs (bp).


Total length
Sum of the lengths of all assembled contigs or scaffolds.


Total length (>= 1,000 bp)
Combined length of sequences that are at least 1,000 bp long.


Total length (>= 10,000 bp)
Combined length of sequences that are at least 10,000 bp long.


Total length (>= 50,000 bp)
Combined length of sequences that are at least 50,000 bp long.


N50
Length of the contig or scaffold at which sequences of that length or longer account for at least 50% of the total assembly length.


L50
Minimum number of the longest contigs or scaffolds needed to account for at least 50% of the total assembly length.


# N's
Total number of ambiguous nucleotide positions (N) in the assembly, usually representing unresolved sequence gaps.





2. Alignment-based statistics (reference-dependent)
These metrics evaluate the assembly by comparing it with a reference genome.







Metric
Meaning




Genome fraction (%)
Percentage of the reference genome covered by the assembled sequences.


Duplication ratio
Ratio of the total aligned length, including overlapping or duplicated alignments, to the reference genome length. A value near 1 generally indicates limited excess aligned sequence.


Largest alignment
Length of the longest alignment between an assembled sequence and the reference genome.


Total aligned length
Sum of the lengths of assembly regions aligned to the reference, according to the tool’s alignment rules.


NGA50
Reference-based continuity metric calculated from aligned assembly blocks using the reference genome length as the benchmark.


LGA50
Minimum number of the longest aligned blocks needed to cover at least 50% of the reference genome.


# misassemblies
Number of structural inconsistencies detected when aligning the assembly to the reference genome.


Misassembled contigs length
Total length of contigs classified as misassembled by the evaluation tool.


# mismatches per 100 kbp
Number of aligned nucleotide positions that differ from the reference, normalized to 100,000 aligned bases.


# indels per 100 kbp
Number of insertion and deletion events detected in the alignments, normalized to 100,000 aligned bases.


# N's per 100 kbp
Number of ambiguous bases (N) per 100,000 bases of assembly sequence.





3. Interpretation guidelines

Continuity: Fewer contigs, a larger longest contig, and higher N50/NGA50 values generally indicate a more continuous assembly.
Completeness: A higher genome fraction indicates that more of the reference genome is represented in the assembly.
Structural consistency: Fewer detected misassemblies indicate better agreement with the reference structure.
Sequence accuracy: Lower mismatch and indel rates indicate fewer differences from the reference, although genuine biological variation can also contribute to these differences.
Ambiguous bases: A high number of N bases indicates unresolved sequence positions, often associated with gaps in scaffolds.
Total length: An assembly length close to the expected genome length can be reassuring, but does not by itself demonstrate completeness or accuracy.

Important: No single metric is sufficient to assess assembly quality. Interpret continuity, completeness, structural consistency, and sequence accuracy together. Metrics such as N50 and NGA50 are not directly interchangeable because they use different reference-length benchmarks.

title: Read a phylogenetic tree
text:
Tips = the genomes you sequenced or downloaded. Internal nodes = inferred common ancestors.
Branch length = amount of change (substitutions per site), not time (unless the tree is time-scaled).
Clade = an ancestor and all its descendants. Rotating the branches around a node does not change the tree.
Root = where the tree starts. Without a root you cannot say who is ancestral.
Support (bootstrap) = how robust a branch is. With ultrafast bootstrap, a value ≥ 95 is considered strong; be careful with lower values.

title: Read a phylogenetic tree
section: What a tree can and cannot tell
text:
What a tree can and cannot tell







It can show
It cannot prove




which genomes are closely related
who infected whom


whether cases form one cluster or several introductions
the direction of transmission


whether a lineage spreads across regions
that two similar genomes are epidemiologically linked
crumbs: Build and read a phylogenetic tree

title: Read a phylogenetic tree
text:
Exercise — read your tree
Open your tree in iTOL (results/phylo/tree.treefile), rooted on NC_045512.2 and coloured by lineage as in the previous page. The collection dates and countries of the references are in the table of NCBI Virus (you can add these columns with Customize columns).
Questions

Where is your sample, SRR26396743? Who are its closest relatives?
Do the references of each lineage form a clade? Is there a lineage that does not?
Which part of the tree is the oldest? Check it against the collection dates.
Which are the longest branches? What do they mean?
Are the bootstrap values high around your sample? What does it tell you?







TipAnswer





Use your own tree.

Your sample sits in the clade of the closest reference found in Lineage assignment. If it is next to a reference of a given lineage, that lineage is a good candidate.
References of the same lineage normally group together. A lineage that is split suggests a labelling issue, or too few genomes to resolve it.
The oldest genomes (early 2020) are close to the root; the tree order should match the collection dates.
Long branches mean many substitutions between a genome and its relatives: either a lineage that evolved fast (for example the first Omicron lineages) or a sequence with errors or missing data.
A bootstrap of 95 or more means that the grouping is well supported. Low values around the sample mean that its position is uncertain: the genome may be incomplete, or the closest references are too similar to be separated.
crumbs: Build and read a phylogenetic tree

title: Read a phylogenetic tree
text:
Final question
Two genomes are identical. List three explanations other than “A infected B”.






TipAnswer






Too few mutations to tell them apart: viruses change slowly, so unrelated cases can have the same sequence over a short period.
A common source that infected both without contact between them.
A common ancestor several steps earlier, with unsampled intermediate cases (you only see part of the chain).
Laboratory contamination or barcode bleed between the two samples.
Missing data: identical on the positions that could be compared (N regions hide differences).




Next: Communicating genomic evidence — module 4.

title: Reference selection
text:
Reads are mapped to one reference, and the consensus is built from that mapping. A reference that is too divergent makes reads map badly (or not at all), hides real variants and biases the consensus towards the reference. For a tree, we also need reference genomes of several lineages to place our own genome in context.







Criterion
Question




Same species / lineage
is it the right virus, the right lineage?


Close to your samples
fewer differences = better mapping


Complete and good quality
complete genome, few ambiguous bases (N)


Well documented
accession number, host, country, collection date


Consistent across the study
the same reference for all the samples you compare

title: Reference selection
text:
Our sample
Our sample is the consensus genome built in the previous exercises from the run SRR26396743:
ls results/consensus/
seqkit stats results/consensus/SRR26396743.fa
Since the mapping exercise we have used NC_045512.2 (Wuhan-Hu-1), the RefSeq reference of SARS-CoV-2, as the coordinate system for this sample.
Questions: what is the length of the consensus? Why was Wuhan-Hu-1 a good reference to map these reads?






TipAnswer





The length should be close to 29.9 kb, that of the SARS-CoV-2 genome. Wuhan-Hu-1 is the RefSeq reference of the right virus, a complete and well-documented genome, and the coordinate system used by the whole community (variant calling, lineage tools, primer schemes).

title: Reference selection
section: Step 1 — Download references of several lineages from NCBI Virus
text:
Step 1 — Download references of several lineages from NCBI Virus
To place our genome in a tree (next sessions), we need reference genomes of several lineages from the same database. Open NCBI Virus: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/labs/virus and choose SARS-CoV-2 (taxid 2697049).

In the filters on the left, keep Nucleotide completeness: complete and Host: Homo sapiens.
Filter by Pango lineage (or add the lineage column to the table with Customize columns) and choose one or two genomes per lineage.
Choose lineages that span the pandemic: the ancestral lineage B (Wuhan-Hu-1, accession NC_045512.2), Alpha (B.1.1.7), Delta (B.1.617.2), Omicron (BA.1, BA.2, BA.5, XBB.1.5) and the lineages circulating when your sample was collected (look at the collection_date of the run SRR26396743 on its NCBI BioSample page).
Prefer genomes with a full date and country, and with few ambiguous bases.
Select about 10–15 genomes, then Download → Nucleotide → FASTA → Build custom, and put Accession and Pango lineage in the definition line. Save the file as data/ncbi/lineage_refs.fasta.

Clean the names (no spaces, no |: the tree software does not like them):
sed '/^>/ { s/[ |][ |]*/_/g; s/_$// }' data/ncbi/lineage_refs.fasta > data/ncbi/lineage_refs.clean.fasta
grep '>' data/ncbi/lineage_refs.clean.fasta
Each name should now look like ACCESSION_LINEAGE. Check that NC_045512.2 is in the list: it will be our root.
Questions: how many genomes did you keep? Which criteria did you use to choose them?






TipAnswer





The criteria are the table at the top of the page: same species, complete genome, few N, documented (accession, lineage, date, country), and a good spread of lineages and dates so that the tree has meaningful comparisons. One genome per lineage is enough for this exercise; real studies use many more.

title: Reference selection
text:
Final question
Why should all the samples of a study be mapped to the same reference?






TipAnswer





Because differences are measured against the reference, with its coordinates. If each sample used another reference, positions would not correspond, mutations would not be comparable, and differences between references would be mistaken for differences between samples. One common reference = one common coordinate system = genomes you can align and compare.



Next: Alignment.

title: Multiple sequence alignment
text:
A multiple sequence alignment puts homologous positions in the same column, so that each column can be compared between genomes. Phylogenetics and SNP counting both start from it.

Consensus genomes obtained by mapping are already on the reference coordinates, but genomes downloaded from public databases can have different lengths, insertions and deletions.
MAFFT is a fast, standard aligner for viral genomes.
Always look at the alignment (AliView, Jalview): never trust it blindly.
Columns full of N or gaps carry no information.

title: Multiple sequence alignment
section: Step 1 — Put all the genomes in one file
text:
Step 1 — Put all the genomes in one file
We combine the lineage references downloaded from NCBI Virus and your consensus from the previous exercises. seqkit seq rewrites the file cleanly, and sed renames the header of the consensus.
mkdir -p results/phylo
seqkit seq data/ncbi/lineage_refs.clean.fasta > results/phylo/all.fasta
sed 's/^>.*/>SRR26396743/' results/consensus/SRR26396743.fa | seqkit seq >> results/phylo/all.fasta
grep -c '>' results/phylo/all.fasta
grep '>' results/phylo/all.fasta
Question: how many sequences are there, and which one is your sample?






TipAnswer





The number of references you downloaded plus one (your consensus, named SRR26396743).

title: Multiple sequence alignment
section: Step 2 — Check the quality of each genome before aligning
text:
Step 2 — Check the quality of each genome before aligning
Count the N in each sequence:
seqkit fx2tab -n -l -B N results/phylo/all.fasta | awk '{printf "%s\t%d bp\t%d N\t%.2f%%\n", $1, $2, $3, 100*$3/$2}'
Questions

Which genome has the most N?
Is your sample good enough to be placed on a tree? (remember the exercise Is this genome good enough?)







TipAnswer





Use your own values. A genome with a large percentage of N (the course threshold is 10 %) has a position in the tree that is less reliable, because missing data can make it look closer to some genomes than it really is. If a reference has many N, replace it in NCBI Virus with a better one.

title: Multiple sequence alignment
text:
Step 3 — Align with MAFFT
mafft --auto --preservecase --thread 2 results/phylo/all.fasta > results/phylo/aln.fasta
(--preservecase keeps our upper-case letters. For a few dozen genomes of 30 kb this takes seconds to minutes.)
seqkit stats results/phylo/aln.fasta
Question: how many sequences and how many alignment columns? Why is the number of columns slightly larger than the genome length?






TipAnswer





The number of sequences is the same as in all.fasta. The number of columns is at least the length of the longest genome: when one genome has an insertion or a different start or end, MAFFT adds gaps (-) in the others so that homologous positions stay in the same column.

title: Multiple sequence alignment
text:
Step 4 — Inspect the alignment
Open results/phylo/aln.fasta in AliView or Jalview (https://www.jalview.org).
Questions

Are the ends of the genomes aligned in the same way for all the sequences?
Do you see blocks of - or N? In which genomes?
Are the differences between genomes spread over the genome or concentrated in some regions?







TipAnswer





Look at your own alignment. The ends of public genomes are often ragged (different start and stop, or poly-A tails), blocks of N come from regions that were not covered, and differences between lineages are concentrated in some genes (the spike gene carries many lineage-defining changes). Real surveillance pipelines trim the ragged ends and mask known problematic sites before building trees.

title: Multiple sequence alignment
text:
Step 5 — SNP distances
How many differences between your sample and each genome? snp-dists ignores N and gaps in each pair:
snp-dists -m results/phylo/aln.fasta | awk '$1=="SRR26396743" && $2!="SRR26396743"' | sort -k3,3n | column -t
Questions

Which genomes are the closest to your sample, and how many SNPs apart?
How many SNPs separate your sample from Wuhan-Hu-1 (NC_045512.2)?







TipAnswer





Read the values in your own table. The closest genomes have the smallest numbers; the distance to Wuhan-Hu-1 gives the amount of evolution since the beginning of the pandemic. Keep this table, we use it for the lineage assignment.



Next: Lineage assignment.

title: Lineage assignment
text:
A lineage is a named group of genomes sharing a common ancestor, defined by mutations specific to that group. For SARS-CoV-2 the standard nomenclature is Pango; names are hierarchical (BA.2 descends from the Omicron lineages, B.1.1.7 is Alpha), so lineages give a common language to talk about genomes without exchanging full sequences.
The references you downloaded from NCBI Virus already carry their Pango lineage in their name (ACCESSION_LINEAGE): they are our labelled landmarks.
grep '>' results/phylo/aln.fasta

title: Lineage assignment
text:
A lineage is a named group of genomes sharing a common ancestor, defined by mutations specific to that group. For SARS-CoV-2 the standard nomenclature is Pango; names are hierarchical (BA.2 descends from the Omicron lineages, B.1.1.7 is Alpha), so lineages give a common language to talk about genomes without exchanging full sequences.
The references you downloaded from NCBI Virus already carry their Pango lineage in their name (ACCESSION_LINEAGE): they are our labelled landmarks.
grep '>' results/phylo/aln.fasta

title: Lineage assignment
section: Step 1 — Find the closest labelled reference
text:
Step 1 — Find the closest labelled reference
The simplest way to give a lineage to a new genome is to ask which labelled genome it resembles most. We reuse the SNP distances:
snp-dists -m results/phylo/aln.fasta | awk '$1=="SRR26396743" && $2!="SRR26396743"' | sort -k3,3n | column -t
Questions

Which reference is the closest to your sample, and what is its lineage?
Is the closest reference much closer than the others, or are several references at a similar distance?
Can you already give a lineage to your sample?







TipAnswer





Use your own table. If one reference is clearly closer than all the others, your sample probably belongs to that lineage or to a sub-lineage of it. If several references from different lineages are at similar distances, the real lineage is probably not in your reference set and you need more references. The answer is a proposal, not a final call: it must be confirmed with the tree (next module).

title: Lineage assignment
section: Step 2 — Cross-check with a dedicated tool (optional, in the browser)
text:
Step 2 — Cross-check with a dedicated tool (optional, in the browser)
Pangolin and Nextclade do this with a complete nomenclature of thousands of lineages and give quality flags (missing data, unexpected mutations). Nothing to install: open https://clades.nextstrain.org, drop results/consensus/SRR26396743.fa in the page and read the clade and Pango lineage it proposes.
Question: does it agree with the lineage of the closest reference?






TipAnswer





The tool may give a more precise lineage (a sub-lineage of the reference that you downloaded), because it knows many more lineages than our 10–15 references. A sub-lineage of the lineage found in Step 1 is a consistent result; a different family means you should re-check the consensus and the references.

title: Lineage assignment
text:
Final question
Can two genomes of the same lineage still be unrelated cases? Why?






TipAnswer





Yes. A lineage is defined by a few mutations, and many separate chains of transmission can carry the same lineage (for example if it was imported several times, or circulated widely before being sampled). A lineage says “belongs to this family”; to say “linked case” you need finer resolution (extra SNPs, as in the SNP distances) and epidemiological information (dates, places, contacts).



Next: Build a phylogenetic tree.

title: Build a phylogenetic tree
text:
Method
Idea
Use




Distance (neighbour-joining)
tree built from pairwise distances
very fast first look


Maximum likelihood (IQ-TREE, RAxML)
the tree that makes the alignment most probable under a substitution model
standard choice


Bayesian / time-scaled (BEAST, TreeTime)
adds time and uncertainty
dating, advanced analyses



Three choices to make: the substitution model (IQ-TREE tests several with -m MFP), the support (ultrafast bootstrap, -B 1000) and the root (an outgroup: a genome that branches off before all the others).
The outgroup must be related to your genomes but outside of them. For SARS-CoV-2 genomes we use Wuhan-Hu-1 (NC_045512.2), the oldest lineage: the tree then reads from the beginning of the pandemic to the recent lineages.

title: Build a phylogenetic tree
text:
Step 1 — Build the maximum-likelihood tree
Find the exact name of the root genome in the alignment, then run IQ-TREE:
OUT=$(grep '>' results/phylo/aln.fasta | grep 'NC_045512.2' | tr -d '>')
echo $OUT
iqtree -s results/phylo/aln.fasta -m MFP -B 1000 -T 2  --prefix results/phylo/tree
What the options mean: -s alignment, -m MFP choose the best model automatically, -B 1000 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates, -T 2 two threads, --seed 1 reproducible result, -o root on the outgroup, --prefix name of the output files.
(If the model test is too slow on your laptop, use -m GTR+G for a first look.)







File
Content




tree.treefile
the tree (Newick format, with bootstrap support)


tree.iqtree
the full report (model chosen, log-likelihood, tree in text)


tree.log
what happened during the run



grep "Best-fit model" results/phylo/tree.iqtree
Questions: which model was chosen? Did IQ-TREE warn about identical sequences?






TipAnswer





Use your own report. IQ-TREE may warn that some sequences are identical (or nearly so): this is normal, they end up at the same position in the tree. The exact model matters little here; what matters more is the quality of the alignment.
crumbs: Build and read a phylogenetic tree

title: Build a phylogenetic tree
section: Step 2 — Draw and annotate the tree in iTOL
text:
Step 2 — Draw and annotate the tree in iTOL

Open https://itol.embl.de and click Upload; upload results/phylo/tree.treefile. (Create an account if you want to keep the tree.)
In the control panel, choose the Rectangular display.
Root: click on the branch of NC_045512.2 and choose Tree structure → Re-root the tree here.
Support: display the bootstrap values (Basic tab, or Advanced tab depending on the version).
Colors: click on an internal node and choose Colors/Styles to colour a clade; colour each lineage (the lineage is in the leaf name) and give your sample, SRR26396743, a different colour.
Export the picture (PNG, SVG or PDF) from the Export tab.

Questions: do the lineages form clean groups on the tree? Where is your sample?






TipAnswer





Use your own tree. References of the same lineage should form a group (a clade); sister lineages sit next to each other. Your sample should fall next to the lineage found in the Lineage assignment page. If it sits alone on a long branch, check its percentage of N and its reference set.



Next: Read a phylogenetic tree.

title: Setup
text: By the end of this page you will have: conda installed, an environment called analyse with all the tools, the course material on your computer, and a viewer (IGV) to look at alignments.

title: Setup
text:
1. Install Conda (Miniconda)
Conda is a program that installs bioinformatics tools and keeps them in separate environments, so that one project does not break another. We use Miniconda, a lightweight, free Conda installer. We will add the conda-forge and bioconda channels to install the bioinformatics tools required for this course.

Linux
Download and install the latest Miniconda installer for your system:
mkdir -p ~/miniconda-installer
cd ~/miniconda-installer

curl -LO https://repo.anaconda.com/miniconda/Miniconda3-latest-Linux-$(uname -m).sh
bash Miniconda3-latest-Linux-$(uname -m).sh
Follow the instructions. Accept the licence and answer yes when asked whether to initialize Conda. Then close and reopen the terminal.


Mac (Intel or Apple chip)
Download and install Miniconda:
mkdir -p ~/miniconda-installer
cd ~/miniconda-installer

curl -LO https://repo.anaconda.com/miniconda/Miniconda3-latest-MacOSX-$(uname -m).sh
bash Miniconda3-latest-MacOSX-$(uname -m).sh
Follow the instructions. Accept the licence and initialize Conda when prompted. Then close and reopen the terminal.


Configure Conda channels
Run these commands once:
conda config --add channels defaults
conda config --add channels bioconda
conda config --add channels conda-forge
conda config --set channel_priority strict


Check the installation
conda --version
conda info
You should see the Conda version and installation details. The terminal prompt may start with (base).
Note: Miniconda does not include mamba by default. You can use conda instead, or install mamba in the base environment:
conda install -n base -c conda-forge mamba

title: Setup
text:
2. Create the Conda environment analyse
If you installed mamba, run:
mamba env create -f environment.yml
Otherwise, use:
conda env create -f environment.yml
The installation may take 10–20 minutes or longer, depending on your internet connection and computer.
Activate the environment:
conda activate analyse
The prompt should now start with (analyse). Run this activation command in every new terminal before using the course tools.

title: Setup
section: 3. Check the tools, one by one
text:
3. Check the tools, one by one
Do not run a script. Type each command and look at the answer: a version number means the tool is installed. If you see command not found, the environment is not active (conda activate analyse) or the tool failed to install — tell the instructor, and see “Plan B” below.
fastqc --version
multiqc --version
trimmomatic -version
seqkit version
kraken2 --version | head -1
spades.py --version
quast.py --version
bwa 2>&1 | grep Version
minimap2 --version
samtools --version | head -1
bcftools --version | head -1
ivar version | head -1
mafft --version
iqtree2 --version | head -1
fasterq-dump --version

title: Setup
text:
4. Install IGV
IGV (Integrative Genomics Viewer) shows the reads stacked along the genome, like a zoomable photograph of an alignment. Download the desktop version from https://igv.org/doc/desktop/ (choose Linux or Mac), or use the browser version at https://igv.org/app.

title: Setup
section: 5. Real data from NCBI (SARS-CoV-2, Rift Valley fever…)
text:
5. Real data from NCBI (SARS-CoV-2, Rift Valley fever…)
The practice data of this course are small, so that every step runs in seconds. The commands you learn work exactly the same on real public data. Here is how to get some from NCBI.

a) Find a sequencing run

Open the SRA database: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra
Search your pathogene, for example:

Rift Valley fever: "Rift Valley fever virus"[Organism] AND "ILLUMINA"[Platform] AND "PAIRED"[Layout]

Pick a result that is Illumina, paired-end, with a small size (a few hundred MB at most). Note its Run accession: it starts with SRR, ERR or DRR (below we write SRRXXXXXXX: replace it with yours). Read the description to know which protocol was used (amplicon, capture, metagenomics).



b) Download the reads
mkdir -p data
cd data
prefetch SRR26396743

title: Mapping
text:
Goal: Align trimmed SARS-CoV-2 reads to the reference genome, evaluate mapping statistics, and inspect aligned reads in a genome browser.
Activate the course environment:
In this exercise, we use the paired-end reads from NCBI run SRR26396743, cleaned in the previous session, and the SARS-CoV-2 reference genome NC_045512.2.

title: Mapping
text:
Step 1 — Index the reference genome
BWA requires an index to align reads efficiently. Samtools also creates a FASTA index, which is useful for downstream analysis and visualization.
bwa index data/NC_045512.2.fasta
samtools faidx data/NC_045512.2.fasta
Questions

What files are created by bwa index?
What is the purpose of the .fai file?
Why do we index the reference before mapping?







TipAnswers






bwa index creates auxiliary index files that allow BWA to search the reference efficiently.
samtools faidx creates a FASTA index (.fai) containing sequence names, lengths, and file offsets.
Indexing avoids rebuilding the reference search structures every time we map reads.

title: Mapping
text:
Step 2 — Map the trimmed reads
Create an output directory:
mkdir -p results/bam
Align the paired-end reads :
bwa mem \
  data/NC_045512.2.fasta \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_1_paired.fastq.gz \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_2_paired.fastq.gz \
  > results/bam/SRR26396743.sam
Convert to BAM and sort the alignments

samtools sort \
  -@ 2 \
  -o results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam \
  results/bam/SRR26396743.sam
Index the sorted BAM file:
samtools index results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam
Calculate the mapping statistics and save them:
samtools flagstat results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam  > results/bam/SRR26396743.flagstat.txt
What do these commands do?

bwa mem aligns the paired-end reads to the reference genome.
-t 2 uses two threads for BWA.
-R adds read-group information, including the run and sample identifiers.
samtools sort sorts alignments by genomic coordinate and writes a BAM file.
samtools index creates an index for the BAM file.
samtools flagstat summarizes alignment and pairing statistics.

Questions

What is the difference between a FASTQ file and a BAM file?
Why do we use a reference genome?
Why are the reads sorted after alignment?







TipAnswers





FASTQ files contain read sequences and their base-quality scores. BAM files contain alignment records, including read positions, mapping information, and flags.
The reference genome provides the coordinate system used to locate reads along the viral genome.
Sorting arranges the alignments by genomic position, making downstream analysis and regional access more efficient.

title: Mapping
text:
Step 3 — Read the mapping statistics
Display the report:
cat results/bam/SRR26396743.flagstat.txt






TipPay particular attention to these lines:




in total: total number of alignment records examined.
mapped: number and percentage of mapped alignment records.
properly paired: number and percentage of records belonging to pairs aligned in the expected orientation and distance.
primary: primary alignment records, excluding secondary and supplementary alignments.









TipAlignment Quality Assessment





After mapping the paired-end reads to the SARS-CoV-2 reference genome using BWA-MEM, samtools flagstat was used to summarize the alignment results.








Metric
Result
Meaning




Total reads
662,332
Total number of alignment records, including primary, secondary, and supplementary records.


Primary alignments
659,100
Number of primary alignment records, representing the main alignment for each read.


Secondary alignments
0
No secondary alignment records were reported.


Supplementary alignments
3,232
Additional alignment records for reads whose alignments are split across multiple genomic regions.


Duplicates
0
No reads were marked as duplicates in this BAM file. This does not prove that PCR or optical duplicates are absent.


Mapped reads
662,193 (99.98%)
Percentage of alignment records classified as mapped.


Primary mapped reads
658,961 (99.98%)
Percentage of primary alignment records classified as mapped.


Paired reads
659,100
Number of primary records identified as belonging to paired-end sequencing data.


Read 1
329,550
Number of primary records identified as the first mate.


Read 2
329,550
Number of primary records identified as the second mate.


Properly paired
640,776 (97.22%)
Number of reads whose pairs satisfy BWA-MEM’s expected pairing criteria.


Both mates mapped
658,958
Number of primary reads for which both the read and its mate are mapped.


Singletons
3 (0.00%)
Number of primary reads mapped while their mate is unmapped.




Interpretation
Mapping rate: Approximately 99.98% of primary reads mapped to the reference genome. This high mapping rate indicates that the reads are highly compatible with the SARS-CoV-2 reference sequence.
Properly paired reads: Approximately 97.22% of primary reads were classified as properly paired. This suggests that most read pairs have an expected orientation and insert size.
Supplementary alignments: The 3,232 supplementary records represent additional alignments, often produced when a read aligns in multiple segments. These are alignment records, not necessarily additional sequencing reads.
Singletons: Only three primary reads were mapped while their mates were unmapped, representing a very small fraction of the data.
Important limitation: A high mapping rate does not, by itself, confirm that the genome assembly is complete or that all mapped bases are accurate. Coverage depth, coverage uniformity, mapping quality, and variant-level evidence should also be examined.




Remember that samtools flagstat reports alignment records, not necessarily read pairs. For paired-end data, one read pair normally produces two alignment records.
You can also obtain a compact summary of the BAM file:
samtools idxstats results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam
The output lists reference sequences, their lengths, the number of mapped records, and the number of unmapped records associated with each reference.

title: Mapping
section: Step 4 — Visualize the alignments in IGV
text:
Step 4 — Visualize the alignments in IGV
IGV (Integrative Genomics Viewer) allows you to inspect aligned reads and compare their bases with the reference genome.
First, confirm that both the BAM file and its index exist:
ls -lh results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam*
Open IGV and load the reference genome:

Select Genomes → Load Genome from File…
Choose data/NC_045512.2.fasta.
Select File → Load from File…
Load results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam.
Navigate to a genomic region by entering a coordinate, for example NC_045512.2:1000-2000, if that is the chromosome label displayed by IGV.

Zoom in to examine individual reads and their mismatches relative to the reference.
Questions

Do the reads cover the whole reference genome or only some regions?
Can you see bases that differ from the reference?
Are the differences supported by multiple reads?
Do the supporting reads have good base quality?
Can you conclude that a mismatch is a true variant simply because it appears in one read?

title: Mapping
text:
Step 5 — Explore read coverage
mkdir -p results/coverage
Use Samtools to calculate the number of reads covering each reference position:
samtools depth -aa results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam \
  > results/coverage/SRR26396743.depth.tsv
Obtain a summary with Samtools:
samtools coverage results/bam/SRR26396743.sorted.bam

Calculate the mean depth across the reference, including positions with zero coverage:
awk '{sum += $3; n++} END {
  if (n > 0) printf "Mean depth: %.2f\n", sum/n;
  else print "No positions found"
}' results/bam/SRR26396743.depth.tsv
Calculate the proportion of reference positions covered by at least one read:
awk '{total++; if ($3 > 0) covered++}
END {
  if (total > 0)
    printf "Reference covered: %.2f%%\n", 100*covered/total;
  else
    print "No positions found"
}' results/bam/SRR26396743.depth.tsv
